newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy unions tell govt to wait over welfare talks.
newsitem.headline: Italy unions tell govt to wait over welfare talks.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi met union leaders on Tuesday for the first round of talks over controversial welfare reform which economists say is vital if Italy is to join the single European currency.

However, the heads of Italy's big three trades union federations told Prodi they would not start full negotiations until the government released its latest package of three-year economic targets (DPEF).
Prodi had hoped to sound out the unions' position on the sensitive welfare issue before putting the final touches to the DPEF, which is due to be unveiled by the end of the month.

The document is expected to give some indication of how much money the government hopes to raise from a reform of social spending, which has moved to the top of the political agenda in Rome following recent warnings about Italy's deficit outlook.

"Without a precise clarification about the state of accounts we cannot continue the talks," Sergio D'Antoni, leader of the Cisl union, told reporters after meeting Prodi and senior ministers, including Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi.
He added that the government should have drawn up a draft outline of the DPEF in the next few days and said he expected to meet ministers again next week to discuss the welfare problem.

Rome has been told by numerous organisations, including the International Monetary Fund, that it must cut social spending if it wants to reduce the deficit in a lasting way and earn a place in European economic and monetary union (EMU) at its 1999 start.

Italy's deficit was 6.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 and the government has introduced some 78 trillion lire ($46.7 billion) of cuts in recent months to reach the three percent goal for 1997 to comply with the Maastricht Treaty.

However, many of the measures are of a one-off nature and to ensure heavily-indebted Italy stays below the three percent threshold in future years, many economists say social spending, especially pension benefits, must be reduced.

But both the unions and Prodi's parliamentary ally, the hard-left Communist Refoundation, have said they will block any attempts to cut social spending and negotiations leading to any meaningful reform are likely to take a long time.
"We'll need months before we reach an agreement, and in any case we shall only talk about pensions at the end of the talks," Sergio Cofferati, head of the Cgil union, said recently.
The government wants to include welfare reforms in the 1998 budget package, which must be presented by the end of September.

Italy actually spends less than the European Union average on welfare, but many analysts believe the system is deeply unbalanced, with much of the cash earmarked for pensions at a time when the population is rapidly ageing.

On present trends, Italy's pensions bill is set to climb by 50 percent in 2010 before doubling again by 2030. Meanwhile, Italy's population between the ages of 15 and 70 is seen plunging to 36.68 million in 2030 from 42.86 million in 1995.
State pensions body Inps is running an annual deficit of around 80 trillion lire and unless things change, this is set to balloon given the population dynamics. ($1 = 1,679 lire)
